title: Grand Canal (Venice)
wiki_lead:
The Grand Canal (Italian: Canal Grande [kaˌnal ˈɡrande], locally and informally Canalazzo; Venetian: Canal Grando, locally usually Canałaso [kanaˈɰaso]) is the largest channel in Venice, Italy, forming one of the major water-traffic corridors in the city.
One end of the canal leads into the lagoon near the Santa Lucia railway station and the other end leads into the basin at San Marco; in between, it makes a large reverse-S shape through the central districts (sestieri) of Venice. It is 3.8 kilometres (2.4 miles) long, and 30 to 90 metres (98 to 295 ft) wide, with an average depth of 5 metres (16 feet).
wiki_excerpt:
The Grand Canal (Italian: Canal Grande [kaˌnal ˈɡrande], locally and informally Canalazzo; Venetian: Canal Grando, locally usually Canałaso [kanaˈɰaso]) is the largest channel in Venice, Italy, forming one of the major water-traffic corridors in the city.
One end of the canal leads into the lagoon near the Santa Lucia railway station and the other end leads into the basin at San Marco; in between, it makes a large reverse-S shape through the central districts (sestieri) of Venice. It is 3.8 kilometres (2.4 miles) long, and 30 to 90 metres (98 to 295 ft) wide, with an average depth of 5 metres (16 feet).


Description

The banks of the Grand Canal are lined with more than 170 buildings, most of which date from the 13th to the 18th century, and demonstrate the welfare and art created by the Republic of Venice. The noble Venetian families faced huge expenses to show off their richness in suitable palazzos; this contest reveals the citizens’ pride and the deep bond with the lagoon. Amongst the many are the Palazzi Barbaro, Ca' Rezzonico, Ca' d'Oro, Palazzo Dario, Ca' Foscari, Palazzo Barbarigo and to Palazzo Venier dei Leoni, housing the Peggy Guggenheim Collection. The churches along the canal include the basilica of Santa Maria della Salute. Centuries-old traditions, such as the Historical Regatta, are perpetuated every year along the Canal.
Because most of the city's traffic goes along the Canal rather than across it, only one bridge crossed the canal until the 19th century, the Rialto Bridge. There are currently three more bridges, the Ponte degli Scalzi, the Ponte dell'Accademia, and the controversial Ponte della Costituzione from 2008, designed by Santiago Calatrava, connecting the train station to Piazzale Roma, one of the few places in Venice where buses and cars can enter. As was usual in the past, people can still take a ferry ride across the canal at several points by standing up on the deck of a simple gondola called a traghetto, although this service is less common than even a decade ago.
Most of the palaces emerge from water without pavement. Consequently, one can only tour past the fronts of the buildings on the grand canal by boat.


History


The first settlements
The Grand Canal probably follows the course of an ancient river (possibly a branch of the Brenta) flowing into the lagoon. Adriatic Veneti groups already lived beside the formerly-named "Rio Businiacus" before the Roman age. They lived in stilt houses and relied on fishing and commerce (mainly salt). Under the rule of the Roman Empire and later of the Byzantine Empire the lagoon became populated and important, and in the early 9th century the doge moved his seat from Malamocco to the safer "Rivoaltus".

grok_lead: The Grand Canal (Italian: Canalazzo; Venetian: Canal GrÃ²nde) is the primary waterway traversing the historic center of Venice, Italy, in a reverse S-shaped path that divides the city into two roughly equal halves, extending from Piazzale Roma near the Santa Lucia railway station to the Bacino di San Marco adjacent to Saint Mark's Square. It measures approximately 3.8 kilometers (2.36 miles) in length, with widths varying between 30 meters (98 feet) at its narrowest points and 90 meters (295 feet) at its widest, and an average depth of 5 meters (16 feet). The canal's tidal waters connect to the Venetian Lagoon and Adriatic Sea, facilitating a natural ebb and flow that changes approximately every 6 hours and 12 minutes. Historically, the Grand Canal originated as the course of an ancient river, possibly a branch of the Brenta, and became integral to Venice's growth as early as the 8th century with initial settlements around the Rialto area, evolving into a bustling trade hub by the 10th century during the city's rise as a major maritime power. Construction of the grand palaces lining its banks accelerated from the 12th to 18th centuries, reflecting the wealth accumulated by Venetian merchants and nobles through commerce with the East and Mediterranean. These over 170 structures, many serving originally as residences ( palazzi) or trading warehouses ( fonteghi), exemplify the architectural evolution of the Venetian Republic, incorporating elements from Byzantine, Gothic, Renaissance, Baroque, and later Neoclassical styles. Among the canal's most notable features are its four bridges, which span its length: the iconic Rialto Bridge, a stone arch completed in 1591 that once hosted markets and shops; the Ponte degli Scalzi, a 1934 stone structure near the church of Santa Maria di Nazareth; the wooden Ponte dell'Accademia from 1933 linking to the Gallerie dell'Accademia; and the modern glass-and-steel Ponte della Costituzione (also known as the Calatrava Bridge), inaugurated in 2008 near Piazzale Roma. Standout buildings include the 15th-century Ca' da Mosto, one of the oldest palaces in Venetian-Byzantine style; the opulent Gothic Ca' d'Oro (1428); the Renaissance Palazzo Dario (1487â1501); and the unfinished Palazzo Venier dei Leoni, now housing the Peggy Guggenheim Collection. At the canal's southeastern end stands the Baroque Basilica di Santa Maria della Salute (1631â1687), built to commemorate the end of a plague outbreak. As Venice's main thoroughfare for waterborne transport, the Grand Canal today accommodates vaporettos (public water buses), private water taxis, gondolas, and traghetti (ferry gondolas), while serving as a venue for annual events like the Regata Storica, a historic boat procession held on the first Sunday of September. The waterway remains a UNESCO World Heritage component within the broader Venice and its Lagoon site, underscoring its enduring role in preserving the city's unique urban fabric and cultural heritage.
